title: Retail Pullback Liquidity
market_niche: Liquid ETFs and large stocks after short-term downside pressure.
phenomenon: Short-horizon oversold conditions may rebound when temporary selling pressure fades.
counterparty_or_forced_actor: Volatility-sensitive sellers, de-risking retail traders, stop-loss clusters, and short-horizon systematic deleveraging.
why_edge_might_exist: Urgent selling can temporarily push prices away from short-term equilibrium, creating a rebound window after forced liquidity demand fades.
why_large_funds_might_ignore_it: The edge may be small, capacity-limited outside liquid ETFs, noisy, turnover-heavy, and hard to scale after spread and market-impact assumptions.

institutional_constraint_evidence.estimated_position_size: unknown until the universe is specified

expected_capacity: Potentially moderate in ETFs and much lower in smaller equities.
persistence_mechanism: Liquidity demand, stop-outs, and behavioral overreaction may recur across market regimes.
crowding_risk: Medium; short-term reversal is well known but implementation details and capacity constraints matter.
edge_decay_trigger: The thesis weakens if rebounds disappear after realistic costs across multiple market regimes or only work after extensive threshold tuning.
observable_prediction: A prespecified pullback rule should improve risk-adjusted return or exposure efficiency without relying on many tuned variants.
falsification_tests: Reject the tested hypothesis if Sharpe does not improve after realistic costs.
Weaken the thesis if results require many thresholds or one lucky date window.
Treat the thesis as untested if the rule has too few trades to evaluate.
suggested_validation: Choose one RSI threshold pair before running.
Use realistic costs because turnover is the main fragility.
Require minimum trade counts before interpreting the result strongly.
references: Connors and Alvarez, Short Term Trading Strategies That Work
Academic literature on short-term reversal effects
